(D) is unsupported; no prices are given. (E) is too strong; the competitors as a group sold fewer, but one competitor could still have grown.
trap: (B) is tempting because a higher share sounds like more sales, but share can rise even as unit sales fall in a shrinking market.

stimulus: Whenever the water temperature in Lake Avira is above 22°C and the concentration of phosphorus in its water is above 30 micrograms per liter, an algae bloom occurs in the lake. Throughout July and August of last year, the lake's water temperature was above 22°C, but no algae bloom occurred.
stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
choices: If phosphorus levels in Lake Avira are kept below 30 micrograms per liter, algae blooms will never occur there.
The phosphorus concentration in Lake Avira was above 30 micrograms per liter in June of last year.
Water temperature has a greater effect on algae blooms in Lake Avira than phosphorus does.
If the water temperature next summer is higher than last summer's, an algae bloom will occur.
At no time during July and August of last year was the phosphorus concentration in Lake Avira above 30 micrograms per liter.
explanation: (E) is correct: high temperature together with high phosphorus guarantees a bloom. Temperature was high throughout July and August, so if phosphorus had been above 30 at any point then, a bloom would have occurred. Since none did, phosphorus stayed at or below 30 the whole time. (A) treats the two conditions as necessary when the passage says only that together they are sufficient; blooms might occur in other ways. (B) concerns June, about which nothing is said. (C) compares the factors' influence, which the passage does not address. (D) ignores phosphorus; heat alone is not stated to cause a bloom.
trap: (A) is tempting because phosphorus seems to be the key, but 'whenever' makes the two conditions sufficient for a bloom, not required for one.

stimulus: In Province Q, only households with annual incomes below 40,000 dollars are eligible for the housing subsidy, and every household receiving the subsidy is eligible. Last year, the number of households receiving the subsidy rose, while the number of households in the province with incomes below 40,000 dollars fell.
stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
choices: Average household income in Province Q rose last year.
The rules for receiving the housing subsidy were changed last year.
The proportion of households with incomes below 40,000 dollars that receive the subsidy rose last year.
Total spending on the housing subsidy rose last year.
Some households with incomes above 40,000 dollars received the subsidy last year.
explanation: (C) is correct: all recipients have incomes below 40,000 dollars, so recipients are a subset of that group. The number of recipients rose while the size of the group fell, so the share of low-income households receiving the subsidy must have risen. (A) is not certain; fewer low-income households does not guarantee a higher average, since other incomes could fall. (B) is a possible explanation, but more eligible households might simply have applied. (D) is unknown because the amount per household could have dropped. (E) contradicts the statement that every recipient is eligible.
trap: (B) is tempting because a rule change is the most natural explanation, but it does not have to be true.

stimulus: The Northside Fitness Club offers members a swimming pool, group exercise classes and a weight room. A survey of all of the club's members found that 60 percent of members use the club's swimming pool and 50 percent attend its group exercise classes. Every member answered the survey.
stem: If the survey results are accurate, which of the following must be true of the club's members?
choices: Exactly 10 percent of members both use the pool and attend group classes.
At least 10 percent of members both use the pool and attend group classes.
Most members who attend group classes also use the pool.
At least 40 percent of members neither use the pool nor attend group classes.
Some members neither use the pool nor attend group classes.
explanation: (B) is correct: 60 percent plus 50 percent is 110 percent, so at least 10 percent must be counted in both groups. (A) is too precise; the overlap could be anywhere from 10 to 50 percent. (C) is not certain: with a 10 percent overlap, only 10 of the 50 percent in classes use the pool, which is 20 percent of class attendees. (D) is false as a requirement; at most 40 percent can use neither, and the share could be as low as 0. (E) is not certain either; with a 10 percent overlap, every member uses at least one facility.
trap: (A) is tempting because 110 minus 100 gives exactly 10, but that number is only the minimum possible overlap.

stimulus: Over the past decade in Nation V, the average wage of workers without a college degree rose 10 percent after adjusting for inflation, while the average wage of workers with a college degree rose 25 percent after adjusting for inflation. During the same period, the share of workers with a college degree rose from 30 percent to 40 percent.
stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
choices: The average inflation-adjusted wage of all workers in Nation V rose by more than 10 percent.
The number of workers without a college degree in Nation V decreased.
More workers in Nation V held college degrees at the end of the decade than at the start.
The ratio of the average inflation-adjusted wage of degree holders to that of workers without degrees increased.
Employers in Nation V value college degrees more than they did a decade ago.
explanation: (D) is correct: if the degree holders' average wage is multiplied by 1.25 and the other group's by 1.10, the ratio between them is multiplied by 1.25 / 1.10, which is greater than 1. (A) is the trap: it would follow if degree holders earned at least as much as non-degree holders, but the passage never compares their wage levels. If degree holders earned far less, the shift toward them could even pull the overall average down. (B) and (C) concern numbers of workers, but only shares are given; the workforce could have grown or shrunk. (E) is an explanation the data do not establish.
trap: (A) feels certain because both groups gained at least 10 percent, but a change in the mix of workers can move the overall average in either direction.

stimulus: In a study of 1,000 adults who were deliberately exposed to a common cold virus, participants who usually slept fewer than six hours a night were twice as likely to develop a cold as participants who usually slept more than seven hours a night.
stem: Which of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?
choices: Among the participants who slept more than seven hours, the proportion who developed a cold was half the proportion among those who slept fewer than six hours.
Most of the participants who developed a cold usually slept fewer than six hours a night.
Sleeping more than seven hours a night protects people from catching colds.
Participants who slept between six and seven hours had a risk of catching a cold between those of the other two groups.
If a person who sleeps fewer than six hours begins sleeping more than seven, that person's risk of catching a cold will be cut in half.
explanation: (A) is correct: 'twice as likely' compares the proportions of each group that got sick, so the longer sleepers' rate was half the shorter sleepers' rate. This simply restates the finding in another form. (B) is unsupported because the sizes of the groups are not given; if few participants slept under six hours, they could account for a minority of the colds. (C) and (E) draw causal conclusions from an association. (D) concerns a group the passage says nothing about.
trap: (B) is tempting because a higher likelihood sounds like more cases, but without group sizes we cannot tell which group produced most of the colds.

stimulus: Lumen Corporation's revenue rose 8 percent last year compared with the year before, but its net profit fell. Lumen's spending on raw materials was exactly the same as in the previous year, and it paid no more in taxes than in the previous year.
stem: Which of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above?
choices: Lumen's labor costs rose last year.
Lumen sold more units of its products last year than the year before.
Lumen's net profit last year was negative.
Lumen raised the prices of its products last year.
At least some of Lumen's costs other than raw materials and taxes increased last year.
explanation: (E) is correct: net profit is revenue minus all costs. Revenue rose, raw material spending was unchanged and taxes did not increase, yet profit fell. The only way this can happen is if some other cost rose by more than the revenue gain. (A) names one specific cost, but the increase could have come from marketing, interest or something else. (B) and (D) are each possible sources of higher revenue, but neither is required, since revenue could rise through either. (C) is unsupported; profit fell, but it may still be positive.
trap: (A) is tempting because labor is a familiar cost, but the passage supports only that some other cost rose, not which one.

stimulus: Biologists have catalogued dozens of species in the beetle genus Carabis. Every known species of Carabis is either nocturnal or lives in caves. No cave-dwelling Carabis species has functional wings. Several Carabis species recently found and catalogued on Island T have functional wings.
stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
choices: No Carabis species on Island T lives in caves.
All nocturnal Carabis species have functional wings.
Some Carabis species on Island T are nocturnal.
Some cave-dwelling Carabis species are also nocturnal.
Every Carabis species on Island T is nocturnal.
explanation: (C) is correct: the winged species on Island T are now known species, so each is either nocturnal or cave-dwelling. Having wings rules out cave-dwelling, so those species must be nocturnal. (A) is the trap: the winged species do not live in caves, but other, wingless Carabis species on the island might. (B) reverses the logic; nocturnal species may or may not have wings. (D) cannot be determined, since the passage does not say whether a species can be both. (E) overreaches for the same reason as (A): wingless island species could be cave-dwellers that are not nocturnal.
trap: (A) is tempting because winged species cannot live in caves, but the statements say nothing about the island's other Carabis species.

stimulus: The government of Country R spent 18 percent of its total budget on health care in 2020 and 22 percent of its total budget on health care in 2025. Over the same period, Country R's total budget, adjusted for inflation, decreased. The budget covers all of the government's spending.
stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
choices: Country R's inflation-adjusted spending on health care rose from 2020 to 2025.
Country R's inflation-adjusted spending on everything other than health care, taken together, was lower in 2025 than in 2020.
Health care costs in Country R rose faster than the general rate of inflation.
Country R spent less on defense in 2025 than in 2020, after adjusting for inflation.
Country R's inflation-adjusted total budget fell by less than 18 percent.
explanation: (B) is correct: spending other than health care was 82 percent of the 2020 budget and 78 percent of a smaller 2025 budget. A smaller share of a smaller total must be a smaller amount. (A) is the trap: 22 percent of a smaller budget may or may not exceed 18 percent of the larger one, depending on how much the budget fell. (C) is unsupported; the passage says nothing about costs, only spending. (D) concerns one category; non-health spending fell as a whole, but defense in particular could have risen. (E) is not given; the size of the decline is unknown.
trap: (A) is tempting because health care's share grew, but a larger share of a shrinking budget is not necessarily a larger amount.

stimulus: Last year every customer who bought Pixa's premium camera also bought Pixa's extended warranty, which is sold for all of Pixa's products. Fewer than half of the customers who bought the extended warranty bought the premium camera. Pixa sold the premium camera to 4,000 customers last year.
stem: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
choices: Pixa sold more of its other cameras than of its premium camera last year.
Most customers who bought the extended warranty bought it with a camera other than the premium camera.
Fewer than half of Pixa's customers bought the extended warranty last year.
Pixa sold the extended warranty to more than 8,000 customers last year.
Revenue from the extended warranty exceeded revenue from the premium camera last year.
explanation: (D) is correct: all 4,000 premium camera buyers bought the warranty, and they make up fewer than half of warranty buyers. So warranty buyers number more than 2 x 4,000 = 8,000. (B) is the trap: most warranty buyers did not buy the premium camera, but the warranty is sold for all Pixa products, so many may have bought it with a printer, lens or other item rather than another camera. (A) is unsupported, for the same reason. (C) cannot be determined because the total number of Pixa customers is not given. (E) cannot be determined without price information.
trap: (B) is tempting because Pixa is known for cameras, but the warranty is sold with all its products, so other buyers need not have bought cameras.

stimulus: Pine Hardware hired a new store manager in March after the previous manager retired. In April, the store's sales were the highest of any month in its 30-year history. The owner concludes that the new manager's leadership caused the record sales.
stem: Which of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the owner's reasoning?
choices: It draws a conclusion about all hardware stores from evidence about a single store.
It criticizes the previous manager rather than evaluating the new manager's work.
It assumes that because one event was followed by another, the first event caused the second.
It assumes that what is true of the store as a whole must be true of each department in it.
It treats a condition that is necessary for record sales as if it were enough to guarantee them.
explanation: (C) is correct: the only evidence is timing. Sales hit a record the month after the manager arrived, but the owner ignores other possible causes, such as seasonal spring demand, a local building boom or a promotion. (A) is wrong because the conclusion is about this store only. (B) is wrong because the previous manager is never mentioned. (D) describes a part-whole error that the argument does not make. (E) describes a necessary/sufficient confusion, but no necessary condition is discussed.
trap: (A) is tempting because a single month at a single store is thin evidence, but the owner never generalizes beyond this store.

stimulus: Fitness blogger: Many of my readers have asked whether they should try the FreshStart diet, which has become popular this year. My answer is that the FreshStart diet cannot be effective. After all, the doctor who created it was once fined for misleading advertising about an unrelated vitamin product.
stem: Which of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the blogger's reasoning?
choices: It assumes that because two events happened together, one caused the other.
It relies on the results of a study with too few participants.
It assumes what it sets out to prove.
It generalizes from a few dieters' experiences to all dieters.
It rejects a claim by attacking the person behind it rather than examining evidence about the claim itself.
explanation: (E) is correct: the blogger dismisses the diet because of its creator's past conduct with an unrelated product, without looking at any evidence about whether the diet works. (A) is wrong because no correlation between two events is used as evidence. (B) and (D) are wrong because the blogger cites no study or dieters' experiences at all. (C) is wrong because the conclusion is supported by a separate premise, however weak, rather than by restating itself.
trap: (C) is tempting because the argument feels unsupported, but it does offer a premise; the problem is that the premise is about the person, not the diet.

stimulus: Marketing director: Last month, a survey posted on our company's website asked visitors which brand of running shoes they prefer. Of the respondents, 85 percent said they prefer our brand to any competing brand. Clearly, most runners in the country prefer our brand.
stem: The director's reasoning is flawed because it
choices: draws a conclusion about runners in general from a sample that is unlikely to be representative of them
assumes that runners who prefer a brand will always buy it
confuses the cause of a preference with its effect
relies on the opinion of an expert outside his field
fails to define the term 'competing brand'
explanation: (A) is correct: people who visit a company's website and answer its survey are likely to be existing fans of the brand, so their views probably do not reflect runners in general. (B) is wrong because the argument concerns preference, not purchasing. (C) is wrong because no cause-and-effect claim is made. (D) is wrong because no expert opinion is cited. (E) points to vagueness, but the meaning of 'competing brand' is clear enough and is not what weakens the argument.
trap: (B) is tempting because preference and purchase are easy to mix up, but the director's conclusion is only about preference.

stimulus: Business association spokesperson: The government has proposed twelve new workplace rules covering matters such as record keeping and signage. Each of the twelve rules is inexpensive for a business to comply with. So the rules as a whole would impose only a small burden on businesses.
stem: Which of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the spokesperson's reasoning?
choices: It assumes that all businesses are the same size.
It relies on the government's own estimate of compliance costs.
It ignores the possibility that some businesses already follow the rules.
It assumes that because each part has a certain property, the whole must have that property as well.
It treats an increase in costs as if it were a decrease.
explanation: (D) is correct: twelve inexpensive rules can add up to a substantial combined cost, and the rules may interact in ways that raise costs further. The spokesperson assumes the whole shares the property of its parts. (A) is wrong because the argument does not depend on business size. (B) is wrong because no source for cost estimates is mentioned. (C) would, if anything, make the burden smaller, so ignoring it does not undermine the conclusion. (E) misdescribes the argument, which never claims costs fall.
trap: (C) is tempting because it names an overlooked possibility, but that possibility supports, rather than undercuts, the spokesperson's conclusion.

stimulus: Opponent of a proposed bike lane network: Supporters claim that bike lanes make cycling safer. But after the city of Marlow built a network of bike lanes, the number of accidents involving cyclists there increased. So bike lanes do not make cycling safer.
stem: The opponent's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: relies on evidence from a single city to draw a general conclusion
fails to consider that the number of people cycling in Marlow may have risen sharply after the lanes were built
assumes that supporters of bike lanes have a financial interest in them
treats the absence of evidence for a claim as evidence against it
fails to say how many bike lanes Marlow built
explanation: (B) is correct: safety is about the risk per cyclist or per trip, not the total number of accidents. If many more people started cycling, accidents could rise even while each cyclist became safer. (A) is a reasonable concern, but one counterexample can be valid evidence; the deeper problem is using raw totals. (C) is wrong because the opponent does not mention supporters' motives. (D) is wrong because the opponent offers evidence, not a lack of it. (E) points to a missing detail that would not repair the argument's central gap.
trap: (A) is tempting because one city seems a small sample, but even a large sample of raw accident totals would have the same problem.

stimulus: Agricultural scientist: Twelve separate studies have examined whether the pesticide Florazine harms honeybees, and none of them found statistically significant harm to the bees. Therefore Florazine is safe for honeybees, and the concerns that beekeepers have raised about it are unfounded.
stem: Which of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the scientist's reasoning?
choices: It relies on studies that were funded by the manufacturer of the pesticide.
It assumes that honeybees are the only insects affected by pesticides.
It treats the failure to find evidence of harm as proof that there is no harm.
It ignores the economic benefits of using Florazine.
It uses the term 'safe' in two different senses.
explanation: (C) is correct: studies that fail to detect significant harm do not prove safety. They may have been too short, too small or designed to measure the wrong effects. The scientist moves from 'no harm was found' to 'there is no harm'. (A) introduces funding, which the argument never mentions. (B) is wrong because the conclusion concerns only honeybees. (D) would be irrelevant even if true, since benefits do not bear on safety. (E) is wrong because 'safe' is used only once.
trap: (A) is tempting because industry funding is a familiar source of bias, but nothing in the argument says who paid for the studies.

stimulus: Sales director: Most of the salespeople who rank among our top performers each year have MBA degrees. Therefore, if we change our hiring policy so that we hire only candidates who hold MBA degrees, most of the new salespeople we hire will become top performers.
stem: The director's reasoning is flawed because it
choices: fails to consider that MBA programs differ in quality
assumes that top performers would perform equally well at other companies
relies on a definition of 'top performer' that is too narrow
ignores the cost of hiring candidates with MBA degrees
treats evidence that most top performers have MBAs as if it showed that most people with MBAs are top performers
explanation: (E) is correct: the fact that most top performers have MBAs says nothing about what share of MBA holders become top performers. If most salespeople at the company have MBAs, top performers will too, even if most MBA holders perform only averagely. (A) is a possible concern, but the argument would fail even if all programs were equal. (B) is irrelevant because the argument concerns only this company. (C) is wrong; no definition is given or relied on. (D) shifts to cost, which is not the reasoning error.
trap: (A) is tempting because it questions MBAs, but the core error is reversing the direction of the percentages.

stimulus: Health official: Five years ago, 20 percent of the flu cases reported in our city occurred among people who had been vaccinated against the flu. This year, the figure was 35 percent. This shows that the flu vaccine has become less effective at preventing the flu.
stem: Which of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the official's reasoning?
choices: It assumes that the flu virus is the same from year to year.
It fails to consider that a much larger share of the city's population may have been vaccinated this year than five years ago.
It ignores the possibility that some flu cases were never reported.
It relies on data from only two years.
It assumes that people who get vaccinated are healthier than people who do not.
explanation: (B) is correct: if far more people are vaccinated, vaccinated people will make up a larger share of flu cases even if the vaccine works just as well. With nearly everyone vaccinated, almost all cases would occur among the vaccinated. The official needs infection rates within each group, not the share of cases. (A) is an assumption the official need not make, since the claim concerns the vaccine's results. (D) is a weakness, but more years of the same statistic would not fix the error. (C) is unlikely to explain the change unless reporting differs by vaccination status. (E) is not assumed anywhere.
trap: (D) is tempting because two data points seem thin, but adding years of the same misleading percentage would not repair the argument.

stimulus: Editorial: The school board is considering a new after-school tutoring program for the district's lowest-performing schools. But the program will not by itself close the achievement gap between those schools and the rest of the district, because the gap also results from differences in funding and family income. So the board should not adopt the program.
stem: The editorial's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: treats the fact that a measure will not fully solve a problem as showing that the measure should not be adopted
assumes that the achievement gap has only one cause
fails to consider how much the tutoring program would cost
presumes without justification that differences in funding cannot be reduced
relies on a vague, undefined term, 'achievement gap'
explanation: (A) is correct: the editorial argues that because the program cannot close the gap on its own, it should be rejected. But a measure can be worthwhile if it narrows the gap, even if other measures are also needed. (B) is wrong; the editorial explicitly says the gap has several causes. (C) names a real consideration, but the editorial's conclusion does not rest on cost, so the omission is not its flaw. (D) is wrong because the editorial never claims funding gaps are permanent. (E) is wrong because the term is used clearly enough and the argument does not turn on its meaning.
trap: (C) is tempting because cost would matter to a real decision, but the editorial's stated reasoning fails even if the program were free.

stimulus: Marketing vice president: Last quarter we emailed a discount offer only to customers who had made a purchase in the previous 30 days. During the quarter, customers who received the email bought an average of three more items than customers who did not. The email campaign clearly increased purchases, so we should send such offers more often.
stem: Which of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the vice president's reasoning?
choices: It fails to establish that the additional purchases were profitable once the discount was taken into account.
It assumes that every customer who received the email read it.
It compares two groups that differed, apart from receiving the email, in a way likely to be related to how much they buy.
It overlooks the possibility that some customers who did not receive the email bought many items.
It draws a conclusion from a single quarter of data.
explanation: (C) is correct: the email went only to recent buyers, who are likely to buy more than other customers whether or not they receive an offer. The difference in purchases may reflect who got the email rather than what it did. (A) raises profitability, but the vice president's central claim is that the email increased purchases; that claim is flawed even if the extra sales were profitable. (B) is not assumed; an average effect can arise even if only some recipients read the email. (D) does not affect a comparison of averages. (E) is a minor concern compared with the built-in difference between the groups.
trap: (A) is tempting because discounts can erode margins, but the main inference, that the email caused more purchases, is undermined by how the groups were chosen.

stimulus: An online home goods shop tracks both the number of visitors to its website and its total sales each month. Last month the number of visitors rose 20 percent compared with the month before, yet the shop's total sales for the month fell.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the situation described above?
choices: The shop added several new product lines last month.
A technical fault made the shop's checkout page unavailable for ten days last month.
Most of the shop's visitors arrive by searching for products on a search engine.
The shop's sales usually rise during the months before major holidays.
The shop lowered its shipping charges last month.
explanation: (B) is correct: if customers could not complete purchases for ten days, sales could fall even as more people visited the site. (A) would, if anything, be expected to increase sales. (C) describes how visitors arrive, which does not explain why more visitors bought less. (D) would make the drop harder to explain, unless we knew last month was not before a holiday. (E) should make buying more attractive and so deepens the puzzle.
trap: (A) is tempting because new products change the shop, but more products would normally raise sales, not lower them.

stimulus: Country H keeps national records of cancer diagnoses and deaths. Over the past 20 years, the number of reported cases of a certain cancer in Country H has doubled. Over the same period, the rate of death from this cancer, measured per 100,000 people, has fallen substantially.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?
choices: The population of Country H has grown slowly over the past 20 years.
Treatments for many other types of cancer have also improved in recent decades.
People in Country H now smoke less than they did 20 years ago.
The cancer is more common among older people than among younger people.
A screening test introduced 20 years ago detects the cancer at an early, highly treatable stage, including many small tumors that previously would have gone unnoticed.
explanation: (E) is correct: better screening explains both trends. Many more cases are found, including small ones that once went undetected, and finding them early makes them easier to treat, so fewer people die. (A) suggests slow population growth, which does not explain a doubling of cases. (B) concerns other cancers. (C) would tend to reduce both cases and deaths, so it does not explain why cases rose. (D) helps explain more cases in an aging population, but not why deaths fell.
trap: (D) is tempting because an aging population can raise case numbers, but it does nothing to explain the falling death rate.

stimulus: When gasoline prices rose sharply in Country K last year, sales of large, fuel-hungry new cars fell compared with the year before. Yet the total number of new cars of all kinds sold in Country K last year rose compared with the year before.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the situation described above?
choices: Car manufacturers raised the prices of large cars last year.
Many people use public transit when gasoline prices are high.
The high fuel prices led many owners of older large cars to replace them sooner than they had planned with smaller, fuel-efficient new cars.
Most car buyers in Country K finance their purchases with loans.
Gasoline prices in Country K are higher than in most neighboring countries.
explanation: (C) is correct: high fuel prices made it costly to keep driving large cars, so many owners replaced them earlier than planned with small cars. That reduces large-car sales and increases total sales at the same time. (A) explains why large-car sales fell but not why total sales rose. (B) would reduce the demand for cars, deepening the puzzle. (D) describes how cars are paid for, which is unrelated to the change. (E) compares Country K with its neighbors, which does not explain last year's change.
trap: (A) is tempting because it explains the drop in large-car sales, but it leaves the rise in total sales unexplained.

stimulus: The city of Dunmore hoped that free public transport would reduce traffic on its roads. After the city made its buses free to ride, bus ridership rose 40 percent within a year. Yet traffic congestion on Dunmore's roads did not decrease.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain why congestion did not decrease?
choices: The wages of Dunmore's bus drivers rose during the year.
The free bus service is funded through a city sales tax.
Car ownership in Dunmore fell slightly during the year.
Most of the new bus riders had previously walked or cycled rather than driven.
The city did not change any bus routes during the year.
explanation: (D) is correct: if the new riders were mostly former walkers and cyclists, few cars left the roads, so congestion would not drop despite the rise in ridership. (A) concerns drivers' pay, which has nothing to do with traffic. (B) explains how the service is paid for, not its effect on traffic. (C) would be expected to reduce congestion, so it deepens the puzzle. (E) is too vague; unchanged routes do not by themselves explain why more riders did not mean fewer cars.
trap: (E) is tempting because route design affects whether drivers switch, but it does not explain why a 40 percent rise in riders took no cars off the road.

stimulus: When farmers in a region began planting a corn variety engineered to resist its main insect pest, their use of insecticides fell sharply. Within a few years, however, insecticide use on these farms had returned to nearly its former level, even though the main pest had not developed resistance to the engineered corn.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the situation described above?
choices: Once the main pest declined, populations of other insect pests not affected by the engineered corn grew, and farmers sprayed insecticides to control them.
The engineered corn costs more to plant than conventional corn.
Some farmers in the region continued to plant conventional corn.
Insecticide prices fell during the period.
The engineered corn produces yields similar to those of conventional corn.
explanation: (A) is correct: the engineered corn controls only its main pest. If other pests then flourished, farmers would need insecticides again, explaining the rebound without any resistance in the main pest. (B) concerns seed costs, which do not affect how much insecticide is needed. (C) is irrelevant because the stimulus describes farms that planted the engineered corn. (D) might encourage slightly more spraying but cannot explain a return to near former levels on its own. (E) concerns yields, not pests.
trap: (D) is tempting because cheaper insecticide could raise use, but a price drop alone does not explain why farmers needed to spray again.

stimulus: A supermarket chain cut the prices of all its store-brand products by 15 percent. Afterward, the chain sold more store-brand items, but the profit it earned on each store-brand item fell. Nevertheless, the chain's overall profits for the period rose compared with the period before.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the situation described above?
choices: The chain spent heavily on advertising the price cuts.
Competing supermarkets also lowered the prices of their store brands.
Store-brand sales rose most in the chain's urban stores.
Shoppers drawn by the cheaper store-brand items also bought more higher-margin products, such as fresh bakery and deli items, during their visits.
The chain's store-brand products are made by some of the same manufacturers that make name-brand products.
explanation: (D) is correct: if the cheaper store brands brought in shoppers who also bought high-margin items, the extra profit from those items could more than offset the lower profit on store brands. (A) increases costs and so deepens the puzzle. (B) would reduce the chain's advantage and also deepens it. (C) describes where sales rose but not how profits could rise. (E) describes how the products are made, which does not explain the change in profit.
trap: (C) is tempting because it shows sales did rise somewhere, but where the extra sales happened does not explain how profits went up while margins fell.

stimulus: Country S publishes official labor statistics every month. Over the past two years, the official unemployment rate in Country S fell from 7 percent to 5 percent. Yet over the same two years, the number of people in Country S who have jobs did not increase.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the facts above?
choices: Many workers in Country S moved from full-time to part-time jobs.
The population of Country S grew during the two years.
Average wages in Country S rose during the two years.
Several large companies in Country S laid off workers during the two years.
Many unemployed people in Country S stopped looking for work and so were no longer counted as unemployed.
explanation: (E) is correct: the unemployment rate counts only people looking for work. If many jobless people gave up searching, they left the count, and the rate fell even though no one gained a job. (A) changes the type of jobs but not the number of people employed or unemployed. (B) would tend to raise the number of job seekers, deepening the puzzle. (C) concerns wages, not the number of people working. (D) would increase unemployment, which makes the falling rate harder to explain.
trap: (A) is tempting because it describes a change in the job market, but people working part-time still count as employed, so the numbers do not change.

stimulus: The death rate among heart surgery patients at Regional Hospital is higher than at Lakeside Clinic, a nearby specialty clinic. Yet cardiologists in the area who are familiar with both institutions consistently refer their own heart surgery patients to Regional Hospital rather than to Lakeside Clinic.
stem: Which of the following, if true, most helps to explain the cardiologists' behavior?
choices: Regional Hospital performs more heart surgeries each year than Lakeside Clinic does.
Patients often prefer Regional Hospital's newer facilities.
Lakeside Clinic's death rate has risen slightly over the past few years.
Within each risk category of patients, Regional Hospital's survival rate is better than Lakeside's, but most of Regional's patients are in the highest-risk category.
Regional Hospital publishes its death rates, but Lakeside Clinic does not.
explanation: (D) is correct: it explains the paradox through patient mix. Regional does better than Lakeside for every type of patient, but because it treats mostly high-risk cases, its overall death rate is higher. Informed cardiologists would rightly prefer it. (A) is tempting, since experience can improve quality, but on its own it does not explain why the higher-volume hospital has more deaths. (B) concerns patients' preferences, while the puzzle is about cardiologists' referrals. (C) is a small change that leaves Lakeside's rate still lower. (E) explains what is known about each institution but not why cardiologists would favor the one with the worse record.
trap: (A) is tempting because high volume often signals expertise, but it does not reconcile the referrals with Regional's higher death rate.
